back: Heating a fat or oil with an alkali (sodium hydroxide) to form soap and glycerol.
fat or oil + sodium hydroxide → soap + glycerol
The sodium (or potassium) salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. sodium stearate.

front: What are fats and oils, chemically?
back: Esters of glycerol and long-chain fatty acids.
notes: Fats are solid, oils liquid, at room temperature.

front: The two parts of a soap particle
back: Hydrocarbon tail: hydrophobic, dissolves in grease. Ionic head (–COO⁻ Na⁺): hydrophilic, dissolves in water.
Tails dissolve in grease, heads in water; scrubbing makes droplets; negative droplets repel and rinse away.

front: How is soap separated from the reaction mixture?
back: By adding saturated sodium chloride solution (salting out); the soap separates as a solid.

front: Main hazard in soap making and the precaution
back: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive: wear eye protection and gloves; wash splashes with plenty of water.

front: Why does soap form scum in hard water?
back: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions react with soap to form insoluble calcium or magnesium salts (scum).
Skin creams and cosmetics, medicines, food and making other chemicals.
